transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Briggs (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Atlas Head of ML), Ethan Morris (Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (Security)

Summary:
Quick scoping to align on pilot milestones, what access Atlas can provide for benchmarking, success criteria for the POC, and a proposed cadence for mid-point and exec readout. A lot of discussion about throughput targets, latency SLOs, and security gating.

Topics:
- Pilot milestones and 6-week sprint cadence
- Access (S3, VPC peering, service accounts)
- Benchmark plan (latency p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens)
- Success criteria and exec readout format
- Security / compliance gating (SOC 2, KMS, audit logs)

Action items (captured in metadata above).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'll kick us off, we're scoped for about 45 minutes but we've got 52 recorded here so we'll try to be crisp
[00:12] Priya Singh: great, thanks Maya, on our side Priya, head of ML at Atlas. we've got Ethan and Lena on — Ethan will talk infra and Lena will handle security follow ups
[00:22] Maya Patel: awesome, Connor from Redwood is our SE, he'll cover the benchmark plan, pairing with your infra folks on access
[00:27] Connor Briggs: hi all, quick agenda — kickoff tasks, access checklist, benchmark harness, mid-point demo, exec readout. also we'll propose success criteria so we can be aligned
[00:39] Ethan Morris: sounds good. just to surface constraints — our prod-like dataset is fairly large, we'd like to mimic chat-like sessions with 1.2k token context, but the bulk of calls today will be on 512 token generative completions
[00:55] Priya Singh: for evals, we want response quality parity with our internal model baseline plus a 30% cost reduction target — not sure that's realistic but that's what exec would like to see
[01:12] Connor Briggs: got it. parity + cost delta is a common ask. we'll propose two benchmark tiers: functional quality (ROUGE / BLEU-ish + human spot checks) and operational performance (p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens).
[01:30] Lena Ortiz: quick sec — security gating, we need to know where model logs go, whether KV cache persists, and KMS integration for keys. we can't have plaintext logs outside our env
[01:43] Maya Patel: absolutely, we have Redwood Private options, and Redwood Dedicated, both can be configured with KMS and audit logs. sometimes transcripts mis-label as 'Redwood Dedicate' in older notes, ignore that
[01:55] Priya Singh: can you explain the difference briefly between Dedicated and Private? we heard both from sales docs
[02:03] Connor Briggs: yes, dedicated is reserved capacity in Redwood's cloud region — you get dedicated GPU pools, no noisy neighbor. Private is full customer-managed control plane, VPC peering or on-prem. for SOC 2 workloads many customers pick Private but Dedicated works if you need quicker onboarding
[02:28] Ethan Morris: onboarding time is a concern — what are typical access steps and how long do they take?
[02:33] Maya Patel: typical 2-week access setup for Dedicated: service account, IAM, test keys, sample runs. For Private, it's usually 3-4 weeks including VPC peering and KMS exchange. for this pilot we'd recommend starting on Dedicated if you want faster time-to-bench and move to Private later if you pass security gates
[02:57] Priya Singh: our exec is sensitive to data residency so I'd like to keep data in our VPC. would Dedicated allow us to keep data in our VPC?
[03:06] Connor Briggs: Dedicated still routes through Redwood infra; you can use S3 gateway + encryption but it doesn't give full control like Private. if residency is non-negotiable, Private or on-prem is the route. we can document tradeoffs in the SOW
[03:21] Ethan Morris: okay that helps. for the benchmarks: we need a harness that can replay real traffic patterns, warm the KV cache, and measure both cold and steady-state latency
[03:33] Connor Briggs: yes, our harness supports prefix caching and can run interleaved cold/warm scenarios. we'll include sample scripts and a README.
[03:41] Priya Singh: timeline wise, what does a 6-week pilot look like?
[03:45] Maya Patel: proposed cadence: week 0 kickoff & access, week 1 baseline runs, weeks 2-3 tuning (batching, quantization), week 4 midpoint readout, week 5 production-style runs, week 6 exec readout and decision
[04:00] Priya Singh: is midpoint supposed to be a technical deep-dive or an exec preview?
[04:05] Connor Briggs: midpoint is technical: runbook, benchmarks, blockers. exec readout is a short deck focused on success criteria and decision points. we can include both if you want — a technical checkpoint followed by an executive summary later that week
[04:20] Lena Ortiz: from security, we need a checklist: SOC 2 artifacts, network diagram, KMS details, RBAC model, retention period for logs. can you provide a template?
[04:30] Maya Patel: yes, we'll attach a security checklist — Connor will own the technical details. note that sometimes the auto-transcripts show weird acronyms like KV cash or kube-pee see, so please assume 'KV cache' and 'kube/ VPC' when reading old docs
[04:46] Ethan Morris: about success criteria — Priya mentioned cost reduction target. we also need throughput guarantees: baseline is 200 tokens/sec sustained for our low latency endpoint and p95 < 300ms for single-turn 256-token completions
[05:03] Connor Briggs: okay we'll include those as targets. just to clarify: p95 < 300ms for 256 tokens and sustain tokens/sec target of 200 for parallelized batch workloads. we'll also surface cost per 1M tokens estimate under different quantization profiles
[05:22] Priya Singh: how do you measure cost? do you include network and egress?
[05:27] Connor Briggs: typically cost-per-token here is inference compute + model weights amortization; for your setup we'll add a network/egress addendum. if you keep data in your VPC with Private deployment, egress is minimal
[05:39] Maya Patel: quick question for the customer: do you have a preferred pilot success score — numeric or binary?
[05:45] Priya Singh: execs prefer a binary decision: go/no-go. but engineering wants concrete metrics. so let's agree on 3 pass conditions: quality parity (>=90% of baseline human evals), latency targets met (p95/p99), and cost <= 70% of current infra cost.
[06:04] Connor Briggs: that's great — we'll build the harness to produce the evidence for each.
[06:10] Ethan Morris: for access — we can provision a dev VPC peering and a read-only S3 bucket with sample data. how do you want service account credentials delivered?
[06:19] Maya Patel: secure upload to our S3 connector or a temporary presigned URL is fine. for Dedicated we'll need an IAM role with limited scope; for Private we'll need the VPC peering and KMS handshake details
[06:34] Lena Ortiz: KMS handshake — we have strict key rotation policies. can Redwood integrate with our HSM via standard KMS APIs?
[06:42] Connor Briggs: yes, we support customer-managed keys and HSM-backed KMS, though the Private deployment is the most straightforward for full HSM integration
[06:52] Priya Singh: perfect. any blockers on your side for starting next week?
[06:57] Maya Patel: none. Connor will prepare the harness and Maya will send SOW.
[07:02] [00:07:02] Speaker 2: (unclear) there was a note about benchmarking with Anthropic models — do you want those included as a baseline competitor?
[07:10] Priya Singh: yes, include Anthropic and our internal baseline; OpenAI can be optional because of compliance concerns, but if it's helpful for cost comparison include estimates
[07:22] Connor Briggs: noted — we'll include Anthropic, our open models, and an optional OpenAI run if you want us to estimate charge.
[07:35] Maya Patel: logistics — we'll aim to have initial artifacts in your Slack channel by Friday, and a shared Google Drive with the runbook and scripts
[07:45] Ethan Morris: any recommendations for sample dataset size for representative runs?
[07:49] Connor Briggs: for throughput and p95 metrics, a modest 10k conversation replay is usually sufficient to generate stable numbers; for human eval we can pick 200-300 prompts for spot checks
[08:02] Priya Singh: on the exec readout slide deck, what metrics should be front-and-center?
[08:07] Connor Briggs: top-line: pass/fail on the three success criteria, cost delta, p95 latency, and recommended deployment (Dedicated vs Private) with migration notes. also a short risk table and any security blockers
[08:20] Lena Ortiz: please include data retention defaults and how to delete logs after run completion — that's critical for our compliance team
[08:27] Maya Patel: we'll add a log retention section and a deletion playbook in the runbook
[08:33] [00:08:33] Speaker 3: small cross-talk about tooling selection (garbled)
[08:40] Priya Singh: last questions: what does the exec readout look like timeframe-wise? 20 minutes? 30?
[08:46] Connor Briggs: 15 minutes + 10 for Q&A is usually sweet. slide deck with 7-8 slides — we can adapt to your exec preference
[08:56] Priya Singh: ok that works.
[08:59] Maya Patel: recap before we close?
[09:02] Connor Briggs: recap: Connor will send benchmark harness and scripts; include Anthropic and internal baseline; Maya will send SOW; Atlas to provide VPC peering details and sample prompts; Lena will start security questionnaire review. Midpoint demo week 4 (2026-11-04 tentative) and exec readout week 6.
[09:24] Priya Singh: yes that's right.
[09:26] Maya Patel: perfect. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and early runs.
[09:31] Ethan Morris: thanks all.
[09:33] Lena Ortiz: thanks.

End of recording.
